passage: I live above the Anand family in the village, and from our balcony I saw their two children in the yard. The younger, Nirmala, stuck her tongue out at her brother Gurpreet after he won the marble game. Her eyebrows were low and she stomped off. A minute later, the same Nirmala stuck her tongue out at him again, this time with wide eyes and a giggle, and ran to be chased. It was the same gesture, but I think it meant different things.

qa.q: Who won the marble game?
qa.a: Gurpreet won the marble game.

qa.q: What do I think Nirmala felt at each tongue-out, and how can I tell?
qa.a: The first time she seems upset, because her eyebrows were low and she stomped off. The second time looks playful, with wide eyes, a giggle and running to be chased, although I can't be sure.

qa.q: What could the parents do if the first tongue is meant to insult?
qa.a: They could teach a kind alternative, such as saying "I'm upset that I lost", while letting playful teasing be.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet feel about the two tongues?
qa.a: He may feel hurt by the first and included by the second, and he might have to work out which one it is each time.

grounding: The same tongue-out gesture can be teasing or play, and the face and body show which.

passage:
Day one: in the Kolkata flat, Tanuja stuck out her tongue at her sister Zeenat when the last mango slice was taken. Their mother said, "That is unkind. Say 'that is my favourite' instead."
Day three: at the corner shop, Tanuja and a friend put their tongues out at each other and both laughed. Their mother let it be.
Day six: Tanuja put her tongue out again at Zeenat during a card game, then said, "I mean it as a joke," and Zeenat rolled her eyes and smiled.

qa.q: What did Tanuja's mother tell her to say instead on day one?
qa.a: She told her to say "that is my favourite".

qa.q: What might Tanuja have been feeling on day one compared with day three?
qa.a: On day one she was probably annoyed about the mango slice being taken, so the tongue was meant as cheek. On day three she and her friend were playing, since they both laughed.

qa.q: What could Tanuja's mother do to help her use kinder alternatives?
qa.a: She can keep pairing a short phrase with the feeling, as she did on day one, and praise Tanuja when she uses words.

qa.q: How might Zeenat see the tongue on day six?
qa.a: She seems to take it as a joke after Tanuja says so, since she smiles, though the eye-roll shows she also finds it a bit annoying.

grounding: Sticking out the tongue can be an insult or play, and adults teach kinder words when it is meant to insult.

passage: The power had gone out on the hottest night of the week, and only the battery fan worked. Abhinav got the spot right under it. Irfan, his big brother, stuck his tongue out at him, long and slow, and turned his back. Abhinav's lip wobbled. Ammi, fanning herself with a newspaper, saw it. “Irfan, that tongue was meant to hurt, wasn't it?” Irfan shrugged. “You're hot and cross. Say that instead. ‘I'm hot too, can we share?’” Irfan mumbled it. Abhinav scooted over.

qa.q: What was the only thing that worked during the power cut?
qa.a: The battery fan.

qa.q: Why did Irfan stick his tongue out at Abhinav?
qa.a: He was hot, cross and jealous that Abhinav had the spot under the fan, so he used his tongue to tease and hurt. He may also have felt it was unfair that he missed out.

qa.q: What did Ammi teach Irfan to do instead?
qa.a: She named what the tongue meant and gave him kind words to use: “I'm hot too, can we share?”

qa.q: How did Abhinav feel when Irfan stuck his tongue out?
qa.a: He was hurt; his lip wobbled, showing the tongue was taken as an insult, not play.

grounding: A preschooler sticks his tongue out at a sibling to tease, and the mother teaches a kind alternative.

passage: Rehana and Kiran knelt in front of the long mirror in Rehana's flat, making faces. Kiran stuck her tongue out and wiggled it. Rehana stuck hers out further and crossed her eyes. They both fell over giggling. Rehana's father looked up from his laptop. The same tongue at the bus stop last week had been a rude one, aimed at a boy who pushed Rehana. Today both girls were laughing, taking turns, eyes bright. He smiled and went back to work.

qa.q: Where were Rehana and Kiran making faces?
qa.a: In front of the long mirror in Rehana's flat.

qa.q: How can you tell the girls were feeling playful rather than rude?
qa.a: They were giggling, taking turns and their eyes were bright, which shows the tongue was fun, not an insult.

qa.q: What did Rehana's father do, and was it wise?
qa.a: He looked at the context and let the game go on; since both girls were laughing together, there was no need to correct them.

qa.q: How would the moment differ if the tongue were aimed at someone who was not laughing?
qa.a: Then, as at the bus stop, it would be a rude signal meant to hurt, and an adult could teach a kinder way to show anger.

grounding: Two children stick their tongues out in play, contrasted with an earlier tongue meant as an insult.

passage:
“I won! Ha!” Rajni clapped.
Bhupen stuck out his tongue at her, eyes narrowed.
“Papa, he did the tongue at me!”
Papa put down the ludo box. “Bhupen, was that a funny tongue or a cross tongue?”
“Cross.” Bhupen folded his arms. “She always wins.”
“Losing feels bad. But the tongue hurts Rajni's feelings. What else could you say?”
Bhupen thought. “…Good game. But I want a rematch.”
“That's much better,” said Papa. Rajni grinned. “Rematch. Let's go.”

qa.q: What game were Rajni and Bhupen playing?
qa.a: Ludo.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling when he stuck out his tongue?
qa.a: He felt angry and frustrated about losing again, and the narrowed eyes show the tongue was meant as a jab. He may also have felt a little jealous that Rajni always wins.

qa.q: How did Papa help Bhupen find a kinder option?
qa.a: He asked what kind of tongue it was, named the feeling, and asked Bhupen what else he could say, so Bhupen came up with the words himself.

qa.q: How did Rajni see the tongue at first?
qa.a: She took it as an insult and went to Papa, but a rematch offer changed the mood.

grounding: A preschooler sticks his tongue out to insult a sibling after losing, and a parent teaches a kind alternative.

passage:
Class note, Friday, from Lakshmi

Two tongues today, two different meanings. At colouring time Swati's brother took the red crayon. Swati stuck her tongue out at him and said, "You're a baby." He looked hurt. I sat with Swati and asked what she felt. "Cross!" I showed her how to say, "I'm cross, give it back after." She said it, and he did.

Later, in the mirror game, the whole table stuck out their tongues and laughed. Swati laughed loudest. 😊

qa.q: What did Swati's brother take at colouring time?
qa.a: The red crayon.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling when she stuck her tongue out at her brother?
qa.a: She was most likely cross that he took the red crayon, and the tongue plus "You're a baby" were meant to tease him. Later in the mirror game the same gesture came from fun, not anger.

qa.q: What kind alternative did Lakshmi teach Swati?
qa.a: To say how she felt and what she wanted: "I'm cross, give it back after."

qa.q: How does Swati's brother feel when she sticks her tongue out at him?
qa.a: He looks hurt, because the tongue and the words are aimed at him as an insult, not as part of a game.

grounding: It shows the same tongue-out gesture used to tease a sibling and later in shared play, with an adult teaching a kinder alternative.
